sc-definition-vs-call.title: Definition or call?
sc-definition-vs-call.prompt: Which line calls an already-defined function named `greet`?
sc-definition-vs-call.hint: A call uses the function name followed by parentheses, without the `def` keyword.

help.concept: A function definition creates the named block of code; a function call runs that block.
help.hint_2: To run the function later, write `greet()`.

sc-function-body-indent.title: Identify the function body
sc-function-body-indent.prompt: Which line correctly belongs inside the body of `def show_message():`?
sc-function-body-indent.hint: Statements inside a function body are indented under the `def` line.

help.concept: Indentation tells Python which statements belong to the function body.
help.hint_1: The body line must be indented.
help.hint_2: The call itself belongs after the definition, not inside its body.

sc-call-count.title: Count function calls
sc-call-count.prompt: A function `ping()` prints `Ping` once. If the program contains `ping()` on two separate lines, how many times is `Ping` printed?
sc-call-count.hint: Each function call runs the function body once.

help.concept: Calling the same function repeatedly reuses the same body each time.
help.hint_1: The first call runs the print once.
help.hint_2: The second call runs that same print once again.

options.d: The function can only be called once

sc-define-before-call.title: Place the call after the definition
sc-define-before-call.prompt: Which program order correctly defines `cheer()` before trying to call it?
sc-define-before-call.hint: Python runs top-level statements from top to bottom.

help.concept: The function name must already be defined by the time Python reaches the call.
help.hint_2: Place `cheer()` after the indented function body.

options.d: put the call before the indented body

function-define-call.title: Defining a function and calling it
function-define-call.bodyMarkdown:
A **function** is a named block of code. Defining the function tells Python what that block should do; calling the function tells Python to run it.

```python
def welcome():
    print("Welcome!")

welcome()
```

There are two different actions here:

- `def welcome():` starts the function definition.
- The indented `print()` line belongs to the function body.
- `welcome()` is the function call.

Python reads the top-level program from top to bottom, so the definition appears before the call. The body does not run merely because it was defined; it runs when `welcome()` is called.

function-reuse.title: Calling the same function more than once
function-reuse.bodyMarkdown:
Once a function is defined, you can call it again whenever you need the same job.

```python
def beep():
    print("Beep")

beep()
beep()
```

Output:

```text
Beep
Beep
```

Each call runs the function body once. The `print("Beep")` statement is written only once, but two calls produce two output lines. This is the basic reason functions are reusable.

function-body.title: Putting several statements inside a function
function-body.bodyMarkdown:
A function body can contain more than one statement. Every statement that belongs to the function stays indented under the `def` line.

```python
def show_card():
    print("Python Workshop")
    print("Room A")

show_card()
```

Output:

```text
Python Workshop
Room A
```

The two `print()` statements are both part of `show_card()` because they share the same indentation. A function can also contain other Python statements you already know, such as assignments, lists, conditionals, and loops. The call remains outside the function body.
